newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 6.50 pct bond yield in sight?.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 6.50 pct bond yield in sight?.

text.p: Several economic reports will punctuate U.S. government securities trading on Tuesday but none are expected to interfere with the market's ability to push higher, analysts said.
The market gets two weekly reports on U.S. department and chain store sales -- the BTM/Schroder's index at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT and the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Retail Sales Index at 1455 EDT/1855 GMT.
The Richmond Federal Reserve will release its June index of regional business conditions at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
The Federal Reserve reports on the level of consumer installment credit for May at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT.
Forecasts for the weekly retail sales measures or for the Richmond Fed index were not available.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that consumer installment credit dropped by $5.6 billion in May after expanding by $7.6 billion in April.

Analysts said the Richmond Fed survey will be of scant interest to investors because they have already seen a nationwide manufacturing sector survey -- the National Association of Purchasing Managers (NAPM) released last week.

The weekly retail sales gauges could attract a little more attention. They are current and they have been offering divergent glimpses of the retail sector, analysts said. The BTM/Schroders index rose 0.1 percent in week ended June 28 while the Redbook index jumped 1.7 percent.
The Fed's May consumer installment report is not likely to be terribly revealing, said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
"I'm not sure that it can tell you what the consumer is likely to do over the next few months," he said.
With reports pertaining to aspects of the U.S. economy expected to have minor impact, at most, the market could very well move higher, analysts said.

"There are a lot of people who are still uninvolved in the market," said Michael Krauss, managing director and chief technical analyst at Chase Securities Inc. "Gold was down $10 (Monday) morning and (ended $6.10) down. The trend has been good. The market's momentum has been good. It looks like we're heading toward (a 30-year bond yield of) 6.50 percent."
Krauss said expectations for a favorable June Producer Price Index (PPI) report due Friday have helped the market.

"There's very little on the horizon to upset the market's apple cart," said Krauss. "There are money flows. Whether they are from central banks or domestic portfolios that are not long enough, a lot will be forced to buy. Money flows are much more important (to the market) than specific news events."
Krauss said domestic portfolios were short of their benchmark durations in April and are now neutral in relation to their benchmarks.
"As long as you have portfolios that are not long their benchmarks and as long as commodity prices stay weak, the market will do well," he said.

Dana Johnson, managing director and head of research at First Chicago Capital Markets, said anticipation of "very good" news on June prices created a "real constructive attitude" that allowed prices to push through some technical resistance and set off more buying on Monday when the 30-year Treasury bond ended at 100-19/32, up 19/32, yielding 6.58 pct.
"The market's going to see if 6-1/2 percent is a viable yield for the long end, whether investors are willing to accumulate positions priced at these levels," said Johnson.
Dealers indicated that Fed funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Tuesday.
